# Part A: report as received

## Scope and interpretation

I included original human-tissue studies of IGH and chronologically aged or photoaged skin. I separated true patient-biopsy observations from cultured-cell, explant, animal, and secondary-data findings. “Not found” means the publication or accessible supplementary material did not report the requested detail; it does not mean the experiment was impossible. For treatment studies, “pigment disorder” means non-neoplastic dyschromia; melanocytic tumors were excluded.

## Idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis

### Melanocyte number and ultrastructure

- Ortonne and Perrot compared affected skin with normal surrounding skin using silver stains, split-DOPA histochemistry, and electron microscopy. The sample was, in the source’s words, “three patients.” Lesions had fewer DOPA-positive melanocytes, rounded cells with absent or fragmented dendrites, and ultrastructural evidence of melanocyte loss. Biopsy size, body site, fields counted, denominator, and numerical effect size: **not found**. [PMID 7377803](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7377803/)

- Wilson, Lavker, and Kligman examined “20 cases” using surface replicas, histochemistry, light microscopy, and electron microscopy across exposed and covered skin. Melanocytes were reduced and hypoactive but not completely absent. Whether exposed and covered specimens were formally within-person paired, biopsy size, counting protocol, and numerical effect size: **not found**. [DOI 10.2340/0001555562301306](https://doi.org/10.2340/0001555562301306)

- Falabella et al. compared “fifteen patients” with “fifteen normal controls matched by age, sex, and skin type.” Routine histology showed epithelial atrophy, reduced or focally absent melanin and melanocytes, flattened rete ridges, and hyperkeratosis. No lineage-specific immunostain or formal cell-counting unit was reported in the accessible record; biopsy size and site: **not found**. [PMID 3805391; DOI 10.1016/S0190-9622(87)70003-6](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/3805391/)

- Ploysangam et al. used DOPA histochemistry and electron microscopy. IGH lesions had fewer DOPA-positive melanocytes, rounder cells, fewer dendrites, and fewer melanosomes. After liquid-nitrogen treatment, repigmentation occurred in “6 to 8 weeks”; DOPA-positive cell numbers were significantly higher in repigmented than untreated lesions, but remained below normal skin. Sample size, biopsy size/site, fields or epidermal length counted, and numerical cell-count effect: **not found**. This was a treated-area versus untreated-area comparison, not a documented same-site pretreatment/post-treatment biopsy pair. [PMID 2229495; DOI 10.1016/0190-9622(90)70273-K](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2229495/)

- Wallace et al. studied “nine lesions” with immunoperoxidase antibodies to c-KIT, tyrosinase-related protein-1, tyrosinase, and gp100/PMEL17, plus double immunofluorescence. Each lesion was compared with grossly normal nonlesional skin. Both KIT-positive cells and differentiation-antigen-positive cells were markedly reduced, reported as “p < 0.0001”; scattered KIT-positive/TRP-1-low cells were present. Biopsy size/site, count denominator, and percentage or absolute difference: **not found**. The abstract names gp100/PMEL17 but does not identify the antibody clone as NKI/beteb. [PMID 9765023; DOI 10.1111/j.1600-0560.1998.tb01761.x](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9765023/)

- Kim et al. examined “47 patients,” pairing lesional with perilesional skin. H&E, Fontana–Masson, MART-1 and NKI/beteb immunohistochemistry showed reduced melanin and melanocyte numbers; electron microscopy was performed in “four cases” and showed degenerative melanocytes and fewer melanosomes. Biopsy diameter, exact sampling site for each pair, counting unit, observer blinding, and quantitative melanocyte effect size: **not found**. [PMID 20465639; DOI 10.1111/j.1365-4632.2009.04209.x](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20465639/)

- Kakepis et al. examined punch biopsies from “four patients” by electron microscopy. Melanocytes and melanosomes appeared structurally normal, while keratinocyte melanosome uptake was focally reduced; focal elastosis was also described. Punch diameter, control pairing, fields counted, and effect size: **not found**. [PMID 25088925; DOI 10.1111/jdv.12646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25088925/)

### Melanoblast and senescence measurements

- Hirobe and Enami studied “five patients” with mini-punch specimens from back, arm, or leg. Lesional punches were “0.8–1.0 mm” in diameter and “1.8 mm” deep; scalp donor punches were “0.8–1.0 mm” by “1.5 mm.” DOPA identified differentiated melanocytes; DOPA-premelanin silver staining identified melanoblasts plus melanocytes. Cells were counted in “10 consecutive sections,” normalized per “0.1 mm²” epidermis, with melanoblast number calculated by subtraction. Lesional melanocytes were “104.7 ± 9.7%” of normal, but melanoblasts only “28.9 ± 4.6%,” reported as “P < 0.001.” Post-grafting assessment was clinical; post-treatment tissue counts were not performed. [DOI 10.1016/j.dsi.2018.04.008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dsi.2018.04.008)

- Rani et al. enrolled “six IGH patients and six controls.” Lesional sites were reported as “4 Legs +2 hands,” whereas control tissue came from thigh; therefore these were independent, incompletely site-matched controls rather than perilesional pairs. DOPA was applied to skin sections, and fresh “0.5 cm × 0.5 cm” grafts were used for melanocyte culture. p16, p21, and HP1 were measured by qRT-PCR and by immunofluorescence on frozen sections, with fluorescence intensity rather than positive-cell density as the protein outcome. All three were significantly higher in IGH; numerical fold changes and confidence intervals: **not found**. [PMID 29516488; DOI 10.1111/ijd.13960](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29516488/)

- Kim et al. obtained paired lesional and perilesional skin, source wording “n=30.” Tissue immunostaining assessed p16, MMP-1, MMP-2, type-IV collagen, and Melan-A; lesional dermis had more p16-positive cells, more MMP-1, and basement-membrane collagen-IV degradation. The p21, SA-β-gal, cleaved-caspase-3 and Ki-67 results were from melanocytes exposed to conditioned medium from UVB-senescent fibroblasts—not from the patient biopsies. Biopsy size/site, tissue-counting unit, and tissue effect magnitude: **not found**. [PMID 31823346; DOI 10.1111/bjd.18801](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31823346/)

- Arbache et al. paired hypochromic lesions with adjacent normal skin from “20 patients,” using routine stains, immunohistochemistry, and electron microscopy. Superficial dermal fibrosis was reported in “90% (18/20).” The exact immunohistochemical antibody panel, biopsy diameter/site, cell-counting method, and melanocyte effect size were **not found** in the accessible article record. [PMID 35114009; DOI 10.1111/ijd.16076](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35114009/)

- Kim et al. assessed paired IGH and normal skin with p16 plus MART-1 immunohistochemistry. Total and p16-positive melanocytes were normalized to basement-membrane length; p16-positive melanocytes were also expressed per “100 melanocytes.” In the linked cohort report, lesions contained “12.3 ± 23.9” p16-positive melanocytes per hundred versus “3.4 ± 6.6” in normal skin, “P = 0.005.” The source cohort was “Fifty-eight patients.” Biopsy diameter: **not found**. [PMID 36394380; DOI 10.1111/jdv.18757](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36394380/)

- The recent ATG7 study found reduced ATG7 by immunohistochemistry in IGH skin, but its single-cell RNA sequencing and time-course bulk transcriptomics were performed on UVB-senescent cultured melanocytes, not IGH biopsies. Metformin reversal was likewise an in-vitro experiment, not treatment of biopsied patients. Human biopsy number, site, pairing, counting protocol, and human-tissue effect magnitude: **not found**. [DOI 10.1093/bjd/ljaf529](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjd/ljaf529)

No published IGH biopsy study using SOX10 as a cell-level outcome was found. No IGH single-cell or spatial-RNA study on patient lesions was found; the ATG7 single-cell work was cultured-cell work.

## Photoaged or senescent human skin — not IGH

Every study in this section is **not about IGH**.

### Histochemistry and immunostaining

- Dimri et al. established SA-β-gal histochemistry at pH 6 in human skin and found age-associated staining in dermal fibroblasts and epidermal keratinocytes. Exact sample size, tissue size, site, pairing, and quantitative effect: **not found** in the accessible record. [PMID 7568133; DOI 10.1073/pnas.92.20.9363](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7568133/)

- Ressler et al. used p16 immunohistochemistry, BMI1 staining, and p16/Ki-67 immunofluorescence in banked human skin. p16 increased and BMI1 decreased with age; p16-positive cells were Ki-67-negative, while overall Ki-67 showed no striking age-dependent change. Tissue was divided into age strata “0–20, 21–70, 71–95 years.” Sample size, biopsy dimensions/site, count denominator, and numerical effect: **not found**. [PMID 16911562; DOI 10.1111/j.1474-9726.2006.00231.x](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16911562/)

- Dreesen et al. compared tissue from “one young donor” with “three old donors,” using IHC for lamin B1, LAP2, LAP2α, lamin A/C, Ki-67, and keratin-10. Old scalp, eyelid, or upper-lip skin showed qualitatively lower lamin B1/LAP2 and Ki-67. Biopsy dimensions, formal count denominator, and effect magnitude: **not found**. [PMID 23439683; DOI 10.1083/jcb.201206121](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23439683/)

- Waaijer et al. counted p16-positive cells in “178 participants” using “4mm” sun-protected upper-inner-arm punches. Epidermal cells were counted along the full dermal–epidermal junction and normalized to its length; dermal fibroblast-like cells were counted by area at high power. Dual p16/S100 and adjacent p16/Melan-A sections in “three participants” supported melanocytic identity. This was cross-sectional, not paired photoexposed/unexposed sampling. [PMID 26286607; DOI 10.1093/gerona/glv114](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26286607/)

- Victorelli et al. used “4 mm” sun-protected inner-upper-arm punches from “20” younger and “41” older donors. IHC/IF included p16, S100, Melan-A, p21, HMGB1, Ki-67 and SIRT1; immuno-FISH measured γH2AX/53BP1 telomere-associated damage. All melanocytes were counted—an “average of 80 nuclei”—along with an “average of 860 keratinocytes per donor.” Older skin had more p16-positive melanocytes, lower nuclear HMGB1 and more telomere-associated damage; p21-positive melanocytes did not change significantly. [PMID 31633821; DOI 10.15252/embj.2019101982](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31633821/)

- Kim et al. analyzed “70” archived specimens from exposed face/neck/forearm and protected trunk. p16 IHC counts were made in epidermis and dermis within “300 µm” of the junction; p16-positive melanocytes or fibroblasts were expressed as percentages of MART-1-positive melanocytes or morphologically defined fibroblasts. Double IF with MITF or FSP1 confirmed cell identity. Exposed versus protected skin contained “6.77 ± 1.54 vs 3.01 ± 0.98%” p16-positive melanocytes and “9.09 ± 1.45 vs 4.98 ± 1.28%” p16-positive fibroblasts. Biopsy diameter: **not found**. [PMID 35151764; DOI 10.1016/j.jid.2022.01.027](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35151764/)

- Burgues et al. studied photoprotected infra-areolar surgical skin from “35 participants”; specimens were “1 cm².” IHC/IF assessed lamin B1, β-galactosidase, p16, 4-HNE, and HMGB1. Ten random epidermal images per subject were used; lamin B1 received a nuclear-envelope score and β-gal/p16 were expressed as percentages of total nuclei. With age, lamin-B1 and nuclear HMGB1 decreased while β-gal and p16 increased. This was intrinsic aging, not IGH and not photoaging. [PMID 42994305; DOI 10.1016/j.acthis.2026.152380](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42994305/)

A frequently cited “photoaged lamin B1” paper did **not** provide human photoaged biopsies: its human component used cultured keratinocytes, while chronic-UV in-vivo skin was mouse skin. It should not be counted as human biopsy evidence. [PMID 29142250; DOI 10.1038/s41598-017-15901-9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29142250/)

### Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics

- Solé-Boldo et al.—**not IGH**—performed droplet single-cell RNA sequencing on sun-protected inguinoiliac skin from “five independent” male donors, using “4-mm punch biopsies.” After quality control, “15,457 cells” were analyzed. This addressed intrinsic aging and showed loss of fibroblast priming; it was not an exposed-versus-protected within-person comparison. [PMID 32327715; DOI 10.1038/s42003-020-0922-4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32327715/)

- Zou et al.—**not IGH**—performed scRNA-seq on photoexposed upper-eyelid specimens from “9 healthy individuals”; the tissue dimensions were “2 mm × 15 mm.” Eleven canonical cell types and six basal-cell subpopulations were identified, with progressive inflammatory and photoaging-associated transcriptional changes. Number of retained cells and donor-level effect sizes: **not found** in the accessible abstract. [PMID 33238152; DOI 10.1016/j.devcel.2020.11.002](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33238152/)

- Zhou et al.—**not IGH**—used paired forearm sun-exposed and buttock-protected punch biopsies from a “single case.” scRNA-seq retained “9,861” cells and identified “25 cell clusters” and “12 skin cell types.” Because there was one donor, between-person sampling error cannot be estimated. [PMID 39540047; DOI 10.3389/fmed.2024.1453940](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39540047/)

- Wyles et al.—**not IGH and not a new biopsy collection**—integrated existing scRNA-seq and spatial-transcriptomic atlases. The reanalysis contained “116,627 cells”; CDKN1A/p21-positive nonreplicating fractions ranged from “4–52%,” whereas CDKN2A/p16-positive fractions were “0–4%.” These are transcript-defined classifications, not IHC-positive-cell counts. [PMID 39370688; DOI 10.1111/acel.14358](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39370688/)

## Treatment-related marker change in pigment disorders

### Demonstrated in human tissue

- **Melan-A/MART-1:** In IGH, post-treatment Melan-A staining after 5-fluorouracil tattooing was qualitative: placebo-treated lesions contained “A few randomly distributed melanocytes,” while treated lesions displayed “numerous melanocytes.” The analysis covered the “first 8 patients,” but there was no pretreatment biopsy and no numerical count. Thus it is treated-versus-placebo endpoint evidence, not true pre/post marker measurement. [PMID 29241792; DOI 10.1016/j.jaad.2017.08.019](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29241792/)

- **MLANA transcript—not a cell count:** In vitiligo, four “4mm” biopsies were obtained from each of “45” patients before and after NB-UVB. Targeted RNA sequencing showed MLANA expression changing from affected pretreatment skin, “0.476 ± 0.745,” to repigmented post-treatment skin, “2.488 ± 0.653,” reported as significant. [PMID 30484529; DOI 10.1590/abd1806-4841.20187589](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30484529/)

- **MITF:** In a paired vitiligo study, “12” patients underwent “3 mm” biopsies before and after narrow-band UVB; MITF-positive cells were counted in two fields, one field per millimetre. The mean changed from “2.5 (2.28)” to “10.42 (3.63),” a mean difference of “7.92 (4.44),” with “95% CI 5.09–10.74” and “p < 0.001.” [DOI 10.4081/dr.2019.8030](https://doi.org/10.4081/dr.2019.8030)

- **MITF and c-KIT:** A recent longitudinal vitiligo study used serial “4-mm” lesional biopsies at baseline and follow-up in “19 patients,” with double immunofluorescence. Epidermal MITF and c-KIT both changed significantly over time after multiplicity correction; MITF reached control-like levels, whereas c-KIT remained reduced. Raw marker effect magnitudes were in supplementary tables and were **not found** in the accessible main text. This is genuine longitudinal tissue evidence, although biopsies sampled adjacent points within the same evolving lesion. [PMID 42941851; DOI 10.3390/ijms27209076](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42941851/)

- **c-KIT and Ki-67, nonpaired evidence:** In vitiligo, immunofluorescence comparing separate untreated and NB-UVB-treated groups—source figure wording “n = 4” untreated and “n = 8” treated—showed restoration of epidermal/infundibular C-KIT-positive melanocytes and more proliferative KI-67-positive melanocytic populations. This was not a within-patient baseline/post-treatment design. [PMID 25822579; DOI 10.1038/jid.2015.126](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25822579/)

- **p16:** In senile lentigo—**not IGH**—radiofrequency treatment involved “Ten volunteers,” with paired pre/post biopsies from “4 participants.” p16-positive fibroblasts decreased after treatment; the numerical cell-count change was **not found**. SA-β-gal and Ki-67 were used for baseline senescence characterization but were not reported as paired pre/post treatment endpoints. [PMID 30279727; DOI 10.7150/thno.26975](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30279727/)

- **p16:** In melasma—**not IGH**—baseline lesional/perilesional p16 assessment included “38 melasma patients”; a radiofrequency pilot had paired tissue from “three” women. p16-positive dermal cells decreased in all treated participants, but a numerical treatment effect was **not found**. [PMID 30575141; DOI 10.1111/exd.13814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30575141/)

### Not found as treatment-responsive biopsy outcomes

For non-neoplastic pigment disorders, I found no qualifying patient-biopsy pre/post evidence for:

- **NKI/beteb:** used diagnostically in IGH and for laser-capture identification in treated vitiligo research, but not as a numerical pre/post marker.
- **SOX10:** not found.
- **p21:** not found; reported treatment-related changes were in cultured or ex-vivo systems, not paired patient biopsies.
- **HP1:** not found.
- **Lamin B1:** not found.
- **SA-β-gal:** not found as a paired patient-biopsy treatment endpoint.
- **Ki-67:** no true paired biopsy study found; only separate treated/untreated vitiligo groups.
- **Melan-A protein:** no true paired pre/post study found; the IGH evidence was qualitative treated-versus-placebo endpoint staining.
  
## What has never been measured before and after treatment in IGH?

Using a strict definition—biopsy before treatment and a second biopsy after treatment with the same marker quantified—**all of the named markers remain unmeasured in IGH**:

**Melan-A/MART-1, NKI/beteb, SOX10, MITF, p16, p21, HP1, Ki-67, c-KIT, lamin B1, and SA-β-gal.**

The closest IGH evidence is:

1. DOPA-positive melanocytes after cryotherapy versus untreated and normal skin, without a documented paired baseline biopsy. [PMID 2229495](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2229495/)
2. Qualitative Melan-A staining after 5-fluorouracil versus placebo, without pretreatment histology. [PMID 29241792](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29241792/)
3. Baseline DOPA/DOPA-premelanin counting before mini-punch grafting, followed only by clinical—not histological—assessment. [DOI 10.1016/j.dsi.2018.04.008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dsi.2018.04.008)

No clinical advice is offered.

# Part B: check of the IGH and treatment sections (2026-11-28)

Checked by a cloud thread against PubMed abstracts (E-utilities), Europe PMC / PMC open full text, Crossref, Semantic Scholar and free publisher PDFs. Paywalled full texts were not worked around. Saved sources are in the project files folder `papers/excerpts/` under the names given below (not committed; `papers/` is git-ignored).

Verdicts: **FOUND** (verbatim in the source), **FOUND w/ diff** (the source says it, with the differences shown), **NOT IN ABSTRACT** (states whether open full text was checked), **DOES NOT MATCH** (the source says something else).

**Totals: 49 items checked. 27 FOUND, 8 FOUND with differences, 13 NOT IN ABSTRACT, 1 DOES NOT MATCH.** No invented paper, PMID or DOI was found. Both unusually high PMIDs exist: **42941851** is Frączek et al., Int J Mol Sci 2026 Oct 13 (PMC13705425), and **42994305** is Burgues et al., Acta Histochem 2026 Nov 6 (online ahead of print). Every PMID and DOI in the two checked sections resolves to a paper whose title matches the description.

## B5. IGH papers new to the project (Gate A candidates, not extracted)

Every IGH paper in the report was compared with `data/search_log.csv`, `data/screening_log.csv` and `data/evidence.csv`. All are already in the search or screening logs except one:

- **Hirobe T, Enami H. Dermatologica Sinica 2018 (DOI 10.1016/j.dsi.2018.04.008). New.** Not indexed in PubMed. It **looks like a treatment study that belongs in the ledger**: the abstract says the authors "tried to treat the IGH macules by mini-punch grafting using a machine (mMG) in combination with narrow-band ultraviolet B (NB-UVB) therapy", with donor punches of "normal scalp skin" placed into holes in lesional skin, NB-UVB started "After 1 week" and "continued", and "Excellent color-matched repigmentation was soon obtained." Five patients. Before extraction: full text is needed (gold open access, refused to the cloud; Ben can save the PDF from a normal browser). Likely problems for the six-month test: NB-UVB was continued, so time from the final treatment may be `NOT_DERIVABLE`, and "soon" gives no time point. Decision for Ben at Gate A.

Not new but worth noting: the full 5-FU tattoo trial (PMID 37011024) is in the ledger; its 2018 preliminary report (PMID 29241792) holds the Melan-A staining and is still paywalled.

# Part C: the checking thread's judgment (not evidence)

This section is the checking thread's own reading, based only on items that checked out above. It is a lead for professionals, framed so that a more full study can be performed by professionals. It is not medical advice.

**What is established in IGH tissue (checked):** lesions have fewer melanocytes than nearby skin in most studies (Wilson "25 and 50 % of normal" at lesion centre; Wallace "markedly reduced", p < 0.0001, nine lesions; Kim 2010 by MART-1 and NKI/beteb). One small study (Hirobe, five patients, abstract) says melanocyte density is similar but melanoblasts are "dramatically decreased", and one EM study (Kakepis, four patients) found structurally normal melanocytes with reduced transfer. Senescence markers p16, p21 and HP1 are higher in lesional skin (Rani, six patients, abstract), and ATG7 is lower (PMID 41453137, abstract). Dermal fibrosis is common (Arbache 2022, 18/20).

**What has not been done in IGH (checked as far as sources allow):** no source checked here biopsies the same IGH patients before and after a treatment and counts any marker. The closest are Ploysangam (DOPA counts, treated areas against untreated lesions), Arbache 2018 (endpoint staining, not checkable) and Hirobe (baseline counts, clinical outcome only).

**A before-and-after marker study in IGH would be new if it:**

1. Took a baseline biopsy and a post-treatment biopsy from matched spots in the same people, with the second biopsy at least six months after the final treatment, so the tissue readout lines up with the project's six-month colour-match test.
2. Counted, blind to time point and arm, per millimetre of basement membrane: melanocytes by a lineage marker (MART-1/Melan-A, with or without a nuclear marker); precursors (Hirobe's DOPA-premelanin method, or Wallace's KIT-positive, TRP-1-low cells); and senescence (p16 in melanocytes and in dermal fibroblasts, as Rani, Yoon and Kim 2019 measured).
3. Settled the baseline disagreement first: are melanocytes missing (Wilson, Wallace, Kim 2010) or present but immature (Hirobe)? That decides whether cell grafting or a melanocyte-activating treatment is the better bet.
4. Paired every biopsy with the objective colour measurement planned in this project, so tissue change and visible match can be compared spot by spot.

**Practical limits to flag for a clinical partner:** IGH spots are "2- to 5-mm" (Falabella abstract), so a 3-4 mm punch removes most of a spot and the same spot cannot be biopsied twice. Sister spots would have to be sampled, as Ocampo-Candiani (repigmented versus non-repigmented sites) and Frączek ("adjacent rather than anatomically identical skin") did, and Frączek warns the earlier biopsy's wound healing may itself change MITF and c-KIT. The paired design in lentigo used 4 people (Yoon, checked); the melasma pilot used three according to the report (not checkable), so pilot sizes in this area are very small. Any such study needs a dermatologist, consent and an ethics board.
